Ouroboros Energy Kinetic Bleed Capacitor#

The Kinetic Bleed Capacitor is a wearable energy harvesting and storage unit that converts ambient kinetic and thermal energy from its user's movement, environmental vibration, and body heat into usable electrical charge. It mounts as a rigid dorsal pack roughly the size of a hardback book, connected via a mesh of piezoelectric filaments woven into a load-bearing vest. Under normal activity — walking, climbing, operating machinery — it accumulates a slow trickle charge stored in a dense graphene supercapacitor array. Under high-exertion scenarios such as combat or sprinting, charge accumulation accelerates dramatically.

What distinguishes the KBC from competing portable power cells is its dual-mode discharge architecture. It can bleed stored energy slowly into connected devices — maintaining a hacking rig, powering a medical automaton, sustaining a signal relay — or it can dump its entire charge in a single directed burst through a contact interface, functioning as an improvised high-voltage discharge weapon or a breaching tool capable of frying electronic locks and sensor grids. This dual use makes it uniquely dangerous in the eyes of regulators, who classify it differently depending on jurisdiction.

The KBC is ubiquitous among couriers, scavengers, and off-grid operators who cannot rely on municipal charging infrastructure. In the deeper residential stacks of GLMZ, where power rationing is enforced by OUROBOROS ENERGY's own metering systems, the KBC is both a survival tool and a political statement — a way of reclaiming energy from the grid that extracts it from you. Corporate security teams have learned to scan for them at checkpoints, not because of the burst-discharge capability, but because operatives use them to power equipment that should be dead.

Ouroboros Energy Laminar Drift Transmitter#

The Laminar Drift Transmitter exploits GLMZ's ubiquitous electrical grid infrastructure as a covert communications medium, encoding encrypted data packets into the laminar noise floor of standard AC power distribution lines using sub-harmonic phase modulation at amplitudes indistinguishable from natural electrical drift and interference. Any building, district, or facility connected to the city's power grid becomes a potential transmission pathway — the signal travels through walls, floors, and conduit without any wireless emission, readable only by a paired receiver physically plugged into the same grid segment. Ouroboros Energy's deep familiarity with the city's power infrastructure is not incidental to this product's design.

The transmitter unit is roughly the size of a thick paperback book and draws its own operating power from the same line it uses to transmit, requiring no separate power source. Encryption is handled by a rotating cipher keyed to grid-segment-specific electrical characteristics — the same transmission on a different grid segment decodes as noise, meaning intercepted data is useless without knowledge of the exact node it originated from. The receiver is a compact plug-in module that can be concealed behind any standard outlet panel. Communication is low-bandwidth but highly reliable, unaffected by RF jamming, signal sweeps, or wireless interdiction measures.

Ouroboros Energy officially sells the Laminar Drift Transmitter to building security contractors and industrial monitoring firms as a 'grid-integrated sensor telemetry solution.' The device's clandestine communications applications are, officially, entirely the responsibility of end users. Unofficially, the system is understood to be the backbone of several long-running criminal and dissident communication networks that have proven extraordinarily difficult for city security forces to locate or disrupt.

Particularly valuable in Faraday-shielded corporate facilities where operatives with physical access can establish a covert channel that exits the building through the power infrastructure rather than through any monitored wireless medium. Also used to establish persistent communication links between fixed nodes in contested urban territory without any visible antenna or transmission hardware.
cultural context The Laminar Drift Transmitter is the preferred communications backbone of GLMZ's older, more patient criminal networks — organizations that have operated for decades and understand that longevity requires infrastructure that doesn't depend on the wireless spectrum that security forces monitor obsessively. There's a generational divide in how operators regard it: younger street-level crews find it slow and inconvenient; veterans who have watched wireless-dependent networks get rolled up overnight treat it as the only trustworthy long-distance communication that exists. Ouroboros Energy's role as the city's primary power utility gives the device an eerie quality — using the grid to communicate means, in some sense, using Ouroboros's own infrastructure against monitoring efforts, with Ouroboros's own hardware.

Ouroboros Energy Pelagic Drift Submersible#

The Pelagic Drift Submersible is a one-to-two occupant underwater transit vehicle developed by Ouroboros Energy for maintenance operations on their submerged tidal infrastructure in GLMZ's harbor basin. Its propulsion system is derived directly from Ouroboros's tidal induction research: rather than conventional propellers, the Pelagic uses a magnetohydrodynamic drive — electromagnetic fields accelerate conductive seawater through internal channels, producing silent, propeller-free thrust. This makes the submersible nearly acoustically undetectable by standard sonar arrays, as it produces no cavitation noise and no mechanical vibration signature. The hull is a double-skinned composite of pressure-rated carbon laminate over a sound-absorbing foam core, shaped in a low-drag teardrop profile optimized for GLMZ's specific harbor current patterns.

The vehicle's operational philosophy is built around patience rather than speed. Maximum velocity is a modest 14 knots, but its power efficiency at low speeds is exceptional — at 4 knots drift speed, the Pelagic can operate for 22 hours on a single charge, navigating passively on pre-mapped current channels with minimal active propulsion. Ouroboros Energy refers to this as 'current riding,' and the onboard navigation system includes a continuously updated map of the harbor's tidal current structure, allowing the vehicle to exploit natural flow for extended range with negligible power draw. The cockpit accommodates two occupants in a reclined tandem configuration, with a small pressurized equipment bay behind the rear seat.

Though officially a maintenance and inspection platform, the Pelagic Drift Submersible has found extensive secondary use in GLMZ's gray and black economy. Its acoustic invisibility makes it the preferred transit platform for moving cargo, personnel, or intelligence across the harbor basin without passing through any monitored surface or aerial corridor. Ouroboros Energy leases units to licensed harbor contractors, but a significant number of units have been acquired through theft, shell company procurement, or decommissioned fleet sales.

Ouroboros Energy Radiant Null Beacon#

The Radiant Null Beacon operates on a principle of controlled electromagnetic contradiction — it broadcasts a precisely tuned counter-signal across seventeen frequency bands simultaneously, creating a localized zone of communicative silence that reads to external scanners not as jamming but as natural dead air. At its core is a micro-fusion cell borrowed from Ouroboros Energy's industrial power regulation line, repurposed to sustain the counter-broadcast for up to seventy-two hours without recharge. The device is roughly the size of a flattened grenade and is typically magnetic-mounted to structural surfaces or dropped into ventilation systems.

What distinguishes the Null Beacon from conventional jammers is its 'ghost signature' emulation layer — rather than creating a detectable wall of interference, it mimics the electromagnetic profile of an inactive urban node, making it nearly invisible to passive sweeps. This was originally developed for Ouroboros's pipeline survey teams operating in contested territories, where communications blackouts needed to appear organic rather than tactical. The result is a device that is terrifyingly effective at concealing coordinated action under the cover of apparent silence.

The Null Beacon has become a fixture in the toolkit of extraction teams, political dissidents, and anyone who needs a meeting to stay off the record. Corporate security divisions have developed specific counter-protocols for detecting them, but the cat-and-mouse cycle of firmware updates keeps the Beacon one step ahead in most civilian environments. Owning one without licensing paperwork is a prosecutable offense in six of GLMZ's administrative districts.

Ouroboros Energy Resonant Carrier Lantern#

The Resonant Carrier Lantern exploits low-frequency electromagnetic bleed from Ouroboros Energy's own municipal power grid infrastructure, piggybacking encrypted data packets onto the 50-60Hz carrier waves that saturate every district of GLMZ. By modulating signal phase differentials at the sub-milliamp level, it creates a covert communication channel that is effectively invisible to conventional spectrum sweeps — the signal looks, to any monitoring system, like ordinary grid noise. The device itself is housed in a weathered industrial casing roughly the size of a thermos, designed to blend into maintenance corridors, junction boxes, and utility tunnels without drawing inspection.

Ouroboros Energy Subsurface Resonance Imager#

The Subsurface Resonance Imager is a ground-contact sensor platform that uses low-frequency acoustic pulse sequences to generate tomographic images of subsurface structures, voids, conduits, and buried infrastructure to depths of up to twelve meters. Originally developed by Ouroboros Energy for pipeline integrity surveys and underground utility mapping in contested excavation zones, the SRI fires precisely calibrated compression waves into the ground through a contact plate and analyzes the return signature to reconstruct a cross-sectional density map of the substrate below. The system can distinguish reinforced concrete from soil, identify hollow voids, detect the presence of fluid-filled conduits, and flag anomalous density concentrations consistent with buried containers or structural intrusions.

What makes the SRI distinctive in the sensor market is its layered frequency approach — it uses three discrete pulse frequencies in sequence, each optimized for a different depth range and material interface, then composites the returns into a unified image. Competitors using single-frequency approaches produce smeared images at depth transitions; the SRI maintains resolution across material boundaries, which is critical in GLMZ's layered urban substrate where decades of construction, demolition, and improvised infrastructure have created a geologically complex underground environment. The imaging software also maintains a growing reference library of known subsurface signatures, allowing it to flag patterns consistent with specific tunnel types, bunker construction methods, and buried infrastructure standards used by different factions in the city.

Outside Ouroboros's industrial applications, the SRI has found significant demand in both official and unofficial contexts. The city's infrastructure authority uses licensed units for emergency subsurface mapping after structural failures. Extraction teams and smuggling operations use it to locate and verify access tunnels, buried caches, and hidden infrastructure. Law enforcement has acquired units for locating concealed spaces in buildings and burial sites in criminal investigations. In the Undercroft — GLMZ's semi-mythologized network of unofficial subsurface spaces — possession of a functional SRI is considered a significant operational asset.

Ouroboros Energy Thermal Glider — 'The Lammergeier'#

The Lammergeier is an unpowered thermal soaring platform developed by Ouroboros Energy as a byproduct of their atmospheric heat mapping research — the company needed a low-cost, long-endurance observation platform for monitoring thermal columns above their industrial energy installations, and the result was a vehicle that accidentally became one of the most capable covert aerial platforms in GLMZ. The airframe is a swept-wing glider with a 9-meter wingspan built from aerogel-composite panels that are nearly invisible on radar and produce no heat signature because the vehicle carries no engine. Lift is generated entirely through exploitation of thermal columns — the rising heat plumes produced in abundance by GLMZ's industrial density.

The Lammergeier's Thermal Navigation System is the vehicle's core intelligence — a suite of atmospheric pressure and temperature sensors linked to a predictive soaring algorithm that identifies and routes the glider between thermal columns with minimal operator input. An experienced pilot can fly indefinitely over the industrial districts, riding the city's waste heat as fuel. The vehicle seats one in a prone configuration, reducing frontal profile to under 0.4 square meters. Communication and sensor systems are passive-only by default — the glider listens and observes without transmitting, making it electronically silent during operations. Data is stored onboard and offloaded after landing.

The Lammergeier is used by Ouroboros for legitimate atmospheric monitoring, but the platform's properties — no engine, no emissions, no active transmissions, radar-near-invisible — make it extraordinarily attractive for surveillance, courier drops, and infiltration overwatch. It is not fast and it cannot operate in rain or low-thermal conditions, but over the right terrain and under the right atmospheric conditions, it is effectively undetectable. Operators who know GLMZ's thermal geography can cross the entire city without touching the ground.

Ouroboros Energy Thermal Stabilization Wrap — 'The Cerecloth'#

The Thermal Stabilization Wrap is a medical device developed by Ouroboros Energy's applied materials division, originally as a byproduct of their thermal regulation research for industrial energy workers operating in extreme temperature environments. The Wrap is a 2-meter by 0.8-meter flexible sheet constructed from Ouroboros's proprietary phase-change thermal composite — a material that absorbs or releases heat in response to temperature differential, actively working to bring whatever it is in contact with toward a target temperature range of 36°C to 37.5°C. It requires no external power source; the phase-change chemistry is self-sustaining for approximately four hours before the thermal reservoir is exhausted, at which point the sheet can be reset by exposure to a heat source above 60°C for three minutes.

The Cerecloth's medical application is hypothermia and hyperthermia management in field conditions, as well as burn wound covering — the sheet's temperature regulation prevents the additional tissue damage caused by air exposure and temperature fluctuation in burn injuries. A secondary application has emerged in the field: wrapping hemorrhagic shock casualties, where the thermal stabilization helps counteract the dangerous heat loss that accompanies significant blood loss. Ouroboros did not design the wrap for this use and does not market it for hemorrhagic shock, but field medics across GLMZ have documented it extensively, and the company has quietly noted the application without comment.

The name 'Cerecloth' is a direct reference to the waxed cloth traditionally used to wrap corpses — a name medics adopted with the characteristic dark humor of their profession, but one that also reflects the wrap's visual quality: matte, slightly iridescent, and conforming closely to whatever it covers. Carrying one is considered practical rather than morbid in most of GLMZ's outer districts, where temperature extremes in unregulated infrastructure zones make hypothermia a genuine field hazard.

cultural context The Cerecloth is one of the few pieces of medical equipment in GLMZ that crosses all social strata without significant friction. Its unrestricted status, low cost, and lack of licensing requirement mean it is available everywhere — in outer-district stalls, corporate first-aid caches, and field medic kits alike. It originated in industrial applications, and in Ouroboros Energy's labor camps and refinery zones it is standard-issue equipment for workers operating near thermal extremes. The irony that a piece of industrial labor equipment became one of the most accessible medical tools in the city is not lost on GLMZ's residents. The Cerecloth has also developed a secondary cultural use: in communities that perform traditional funerary rites, the phrase 'laying on the Cerecloth' has become a euphemism for preparing someone for death when survival is no longer possible — the wrap's original industrial purpose and its field medical use colliding in the city's dark vernacular.

The vehicle operates on a hybrid lift system combining a low-profile ducted fan array for primary thrust with passive thermal updraft exploitation — it is literally designed to ride the superheated air columns rising from the city's geothermal infrastructure, dramatically extending its operational range when flying over active vent fields.

Ouroboros Energy Tidal Frequency Dead Drop#

The Tidal Frequency Dead Drop is a waterproof, neutrally buoyant data storage and transmission device designed to be deployed in GLMZ's extensive subsurface water infrastructure — the drainage canals, flood management tunnels, retention basins, and tidal exchange channels that run beneath much of the city's lower districts. The device drifts passively with water flow until it reaches a pre-programmed depth or salinity threshold, at which point it anchors itself magnetically to any ferrous surface in its proximity and enters a listening state. A courier with the corresponding receiver can make contact simply by moving through the same water infrastructure within 15 meters of the deployed unit, triggering a rapid burst transmission of the stored payload over a short-range encrypted channel that exists for only the duration of the exchange — typically 1.4 to 3 seconds.

Ouroboros Energy developed the Tidal Frequency Dead Drop ostensibly for use in its subsurface infrastructure monitoring network, where autonomous sensor units needed a mechanism to offload collected data to maintenance personnel without requiring hardwired access points. The dead drop architecture — passive storage, triggered burst, automatic payload wipe after successful transfer — was a genuine engineering solution to a real logistics problem. It is also, with minimal modification, a near-perfect covert communication tool. The water infrastructure provides physical concealment, acoustic masking, and a delivery medium that moves payloads passively across the city without any operator involvement after initial deployment.

The device has become foundational to GLMZ's underground information economy. Operators who need to pass sensitive data across the city without courier risk deploy a Tidal Drop into the drainage system at one location and let the city's own water management infrastructure carry it to the recipient's collection point. The 72-hour operational window and automatic payload wipe on successful transfer mean that even a recovered device yields nothing actionable after the exchange has occurred.

Ouroboros Energy Tidal Induction Spool#

The Tidal Induction Spool is a portable power harvesting and distribution unit that extracts usable electrical energy from the electromagnetic fields generated by high-current industrial infrastructure — power conduits, transformer stations, rail lines, and the dense cable bundles that run through GLMZ's building interiors. The device consists of a 30-meter spool of induction coil wire with a shielded magnetic core head, a power conditioning unit that stabilizes harvested current into clean DC output, and a fast-charge distribution hub with six output ports supporting a range of device voltages. The coil head is simply draped or wrapped around a target power conduit — no physical connection required — and the induced current is conditioned and made available within seconds.

Ouroboros Energy designed the TIS as a field maintenance tool for their own grid technicians operating in zones where safe power access points are damaged, inaccessible, or deliberately removed by infrastructure sabotage. The power conditioning unit is the device's engineering achievement: it handles wildly variable input — anything from the 50Hz hum of a building main to the irregular spikes of an aging transformer — and outputs a stable, device-safe current. The conditioning unit also includes a load balancing algorithm that prevents the induction draw from creating a detectable anomaly on the source circuit, a feature that was ostensibly designed to prevent nuisance tripping of circuit breakers but has obvious applications for covert operation.

In the hands of GLMZ's runner community, the TIS solves one of the persistent logistical problems of extended field operations: keeping devices charged in environments where power infrastructure is present but inaccessible. It is equally valued by the city's squatter communities in the lower-ring industrial zones, where 'tapping the grid' is a survival practice that the TIS makes significantly safer and more reliable than improvised alternatives.

Ouroboros Serpent Tongue Relay#

The Ouroboros Serpent Tongue Relay is a secure channel device built around a single conceptual innovation: it routes all transmissions through Ouroboros Energy's proprietary smart-grid infrastructure, embedding communications data within the load-balancing telemetry that the corporation's power distribution network broadcasts continuously across GLMZ. Because the city's power grid is the most heavily trafficked and least-scrutinized data channel in existence — monitored obsessively for energy metrics but almost never for embedded payloads — the Serpent Tongue achieves a form of steganographic invisibility that no dedicated communications channel can match. A transmission sent through a Serpent Tongue relay is, to any external observer, a routine fluctuation in district power consumption data.

Pale Letter Dead Drop Terminal#

The Pale Letter Dead Drop Terminal is a physically unassuming communications device — typically disguised as a piece of mundane urban infrastructure, such as an electrical junction box, a ventilation panel cover, or a section of decorative wall tile — that functions as an asynchronous, air-gapped message exchange point for operatives who cannot risk real-time communication. Messages are composed offline on an encrypted companion device, compressed into a burst transmission lasting less than 0.3 seconds, and physically transmitted to the Terminal on close approach via short-range encrypted radio. The Terminal stores the message in an isolated internal memory with no external network connection, where it waits until another authorized party approaches and pulls it down with a corresponding burst receive.

The Pale Letter's security architecture is built around the principle of temporal separation — sender and receiver never need to be in the same place at the same time, and the Terminal never connects to any network, making it undetectable by conventional signals intelligence. The device's internal clock erases stored messages on a configurable timer between two and seventy-two hours, ensuring that if a Terminal is discovered, the window for recovering its contents is narrow. Physical intrusion triggers an immediate memory wipe. The Terminal is powered by a long-life kinetic harvesting cell that draws energy from vibrations in the surrounding structure — it requires no external power and can remain dormant for years.

Pale Letter Terminals are manufactured in small batches by Ringo Corponation's 'grey infrastructure' division and are distributed through a network of trusted intermediaries rather than conventional retail channels. They are standard equipment for deep-cover intelligence operatives, long-running infiltration specialists, and the leadership structures of organizations that have been penetrated by surveillance operations. In GLMZ's more paranoid underground circles, a network of Pale Letter Terminals is called a 'cold line' — a communications infrastructure that exists entirely outside the city's monitored networks.

Palladian Construction Compressive Load Carapace#

Originally engineered for workers operating in active demolition and controlled-collapse environments, the Compressive Load Carapace uses layered ceramic-polymer composite panels bonded to a semi-rigid undersuit reinforced with Palladian's proprietary stress-redistribution lattice. When subjected to blunt force or crushing pressure, the lattice micro-fractures in a controlled pattern, dissipating kinetic energy laterally across the suit's surface rather than transmitting it inward to the wearer's body. Replacement panel cartridges can be swapped in the field within minutes, making it a practical choice for prolonged operations.

What distinguishes the Carapace from conventional construction PPE is the integrated pressure-sensing membrane woven into the undersuit's torso section. This membrane monitors structural load in real time and triggers passive bracing in the suit's shoulder and hip assemblies when threshold forces are detected, effectively pre-tensioning the wearer's posture before impact fully registers. The result is a suit that responds to its environment rather than simply absorbing it.

On the street, the Carapace has migrated from worksites into the hands of enforcers, debt collectors, and anyone who expects to be in a tight space when things go wrong. Its bulk reads as industrial rather than military, which lets wearers move through checkpoints that would flag tactical gear. Palladian officially sells it only to licensed contractors, but grey-market panel kits and secondhand full suits are common enough in the outer districts that the distinction has become largely ceremonial.

Palladian Construction Crestline Hauler-Rig#

The Crestline Hauler-Rig is a heavy-duty exo-assisted ground vehicle built around a modular cargo spine and six independently articulated drive wheels, each capable of torque-vectoring across uneven terrain. Its onboard load-balancing AI — called the Ballast Cognition Module — continuously redistributes weight across the chassis to prevent tipping on collapsed infrastructure, rubble fields, and the deeply rutted access roads that connect GLMZ's outer districts to its central arcology cores. Power is drawn from a dual-cell hydrogen compression stack buried beneath the operator cab, giving the Crestline a range of approximately 900 kilometers before refuel under full load.

Palladian Construction Loadframe Exo-Rig — 'The Mule'#

The Loadframe Exo-Rig is a full-body industrial exoskeleton developed by Palladian Construction for heavy labor in GLMZ's perpetual construction and demolition zones. Worn as a suit, it amplifies the operator's physical output by a factor of twelve through a network of hydraulic actuators and strain-anticipation servos, allowing a single worker to lift, carry, and place loads that would otherwise require heavy machinery. The rig's steel-composite frame distributes weight across a broad base plate system, preventing the ground sinkage common in soft rubble terrain. Palladian designed the Mule for efficiency, not elegance — it is loud, heavy, and visually imposing in a way that reflects its purpose entirely.

The Mule's Strain Anticipation System is its most technically sophisticated feature — a suite of force sensors and a predictive algorithm that reads the operator's movement intent from micro-muscle activations and pre-loads the actuators before the full movement is initiated. This eliminates the half-second lag common in older exo-rigs and gives experienced operators the sensation of the suit moving with them rather than after them. The system was designed for load-bearing tasks but translates effectively to combat applications, where the pre-loaded actuators allow strike speeds and force outputs that exceed what unaugmented humans can track and respond to. Palladian does not advertise this application.

The Mule is everywhere in GLMZ — construction sites, salvage yards, port facilities, and disaster response operations. Because it is classified as industrial equipment rather than a weapon system, licensing requirements are comparatively light, making it accessible at lower tiers than most military-grade hardware. This has led to widespread adoption outside its intended context. Modified Mules appear in underground fighting circuits, in the hands of gang enforcers, and in the toolkit of any outfit that needs someone to walk through a wall.

Palladian Construction Seismic Anchor Cradle#

The Seismic Anchor Cradle is a deployable structural stabilization platform developed originally for Palladian's deep-excavation teams operating in GLMZ's subsidence zones. The unit consists of a collapsible titanium-alloy frame with six pneumatically-driven anchor spikes that fire into substrate on command, achieving load-bearing stability on surfaces ranging from loose fill to cracked ferroconcrete within 1.4 seconds. An onboard micro-gyroscope continuously adjusts tension distribution across the spike array to compensate for ground shift, vibration, or active tremor events, making it viable on the city's perpetually unstable eastern industrial shelf.

What distinguishes the Cradle from competing anchor systems is its dual-use design philosophy: the same frame that stabilizes heavy construction equipment during drilling operations can be rapidly reconfigured as a personnel rappel anchor, a cable-transit anchor point, or a hard mount for crew-served equipment. The retraction motor is quiet enough to operate without triggering standard construction-site acoustic monitors, a feature that was almost certainly not accidental given how frequently the unit appears outside of legitimate worksites.

Among construction crews it is unremarkable kit, but the Cradle has developed a second life among urban climbers, extraction teams, and anyone who needs a guaranteed anchor point in structurally compromised environments. The spike-fire sound — a distinctive thump-hiss — is recognizable enough that experienced operators use it as a covert signal in the field.

Palladian Construction Structural Echo Tap#

Developed ostensibly as a structural integrity monitoring tool, the Structural Echo Tap transmits data by inducing precisely calibrated micro-vibrations into load-bearing concrete, rebar, and steel superstructures — the bones of GLMZ's perpetually under-construction cityscape. Receiving units detect and decode these vibrations using contact piezoelectric sensors pressed against the same structural members, reconstructing the signal from what appears to any passive observer as ordinary building settlement noise. The system was designed for Palladian Construction's own site supervisors to maintain covert communication channels in environments too electromagnetically hostile for conventional radio, but units have since proliferated well beyond authorized hands.

Because the signal travels through solid matter rather than air, it passes through Faraday cages, RF shielding, and signal-suppressed environments without attenuation. This makes it invaluable for communicating into or out of hardened secure facilities, holding cells, corporate black sites, and bunkers. Operators have developed a practice of mapping structural paths in advance — identifying which columns and beams connect which rooms — to plot reliable signal routes through complex buildings. Voice transmission is possible but degraded; short coded text bursts are the standard protocol.
cultural context Palladian Construction's near-monopoly on major civil construction in GLMZ means their rebar and poured concrete is in virtually every significant structure in the city. This ubiquity is not lost on those who use the Tap — there is dark humor in the fact that the city's physical skeleton has become a covert communications network. Among incarcerated fixers, political prisoners, and corporate detainees, the Tap is sometimes the only link to the outside world, passed in through bribed guards or concealed in personal effects. Palladian has never officially acknowledged the non-construction uses of the device, maintaining that all licensed units are for site management only.

Palladian Construction Tectonic Anchor Spike#

The Tectonic Anchor Spike is a pneumatically-driven mooring device originally engineered for emergency structural reinforcement in GLMZ's chronically unstable lower construction zones, where subsidence, seismic micro-events, and deliberate demolition create environments where conventional anchoring fails. The device resembles a short-barreled pneumatic tool roughly 40cm long, loaded with a single hardened osmium-core spike approximately 25cm in length. When fired against a surface — concrete, reinforced composite, structural steel, compacted rubble — the spike drives to a depth determined by material resistance and locks via a radially-expanding barb array that deploys on a half-rotation of the integrated locking collar. The result is a mooring point rated to 800kg of tensile load in a matter of seconds.

The T-Spike's engineering distinction lies in the barb deployment mechanism, which is calibrated to expand proportionally to the density of the substrate it has entered. In soft material it expands fully and aggressively; in dense steel it deploys at a reduced angle to avoid fracturing the spike itself. This adaptive anchoring means it works reliably across the enormously varied construction materials found in GLMZ's layered architecture — from centuries-old ferroconcrete to the proprietary synthecrete blends used in modern corporate towers. A retrieval wrench is included that reverses the barb array for non-destructive removal, though this takes considerably longer than deployment.

Palladian originally sold the T-Spike to construction crews, emergency response teams, and their own contracted demolition units. The device migrated rapidly into the broader market because it solves a fundamental problem for anyone operating vertically in the city — reliable, fast, load-bearing anchorage in unknown substrate. Climbers, infiltrators, rescue teams, and salvage crews all use it. The pneumatic cartridge is single-use but widely available; the driver tool itself is reusable indefinitely with minimal maintenance.

Palladian Gravemind Relay Hub#

The Gravemind Relay Hub is a distributed mesh-coordination device roughly the size of a hardcover book, constructed from Palladian Construction's proprietary stress-ceramic housing. It operates by seeding a local area with micro-relay dust — particles thin enough to drift through ventilation systems and settle on surfaces — which collectively form a self-organizing signal lattice. The hub itself acts as the root node, stitching the dust-relays into a coherent network that can support up to forty-eight simultaneous encrypted voice and data channels across a radius of roughly six city blocks.

What distinguishes the Gravemind from conventional mesh nodes is its passive topology — the dust-relays require no active power draw, harvesting ambient EM bleed from nearby infrastructure to sustain themselves. This makes the network nearly undetectable by standard sweep equipment, as there is no central transmitter to locate. Traffic is fragmented and distributed across hundreds of micro-nodes before being reconstructed at the receiving end, a process Palladian markets as 'architectural encryption.'

The hub is favored by fixers and mid-tier syndicate operations that need persistent comms infrastructure in contested urban zones without the risk of a single point of compromise. Construction crews operating in corporate exclusion zones use them to maintain coordination when standard channels are jammed or monitored. Law enforcement occasionally finds decommissioned units months after an operation has concluded, the dust long settled into the walls.

Ringo Corponation Adrenal Sequencing Patch#

The Adrenal Sequencing Patch is a transdermal pharmaceutical delivery system designed to regulate, suppress, or selectively amplify adrenal output in patients experiencing shock, combat stress cascade, or acute adrenal dysregulation — a condition increasingly common among individuals with heavy autonomic cyberware integration. Applied to the neck or inner wrist, the patch deploys a micro-needle array that anchors to the dermis and begins continuous bloodstream sampling within ninety seconds. A small embedded logic unit reads cortisol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine levels in real time and responds by releasing one of three pre-loaded pharmaceutical payloads: a suppressant blend for hyperadrenal crisis, a regulated stimulant for adrenal insufficiency or shock, or a stabilizing neutral compound that simply floors the variance and holds the patient at functional baseline.

Ringo Corponation developed the Sequencing Patch primarily for their own corporate security and high-stress executive protection programs — environments where personnel needed to remain functional and decision-capable under sustained threat rather than simply surviving. The patch's distinctive feature is its feedback loop: rather than a fixed dose, it titrates continuously, making hundreds of micro-adjustments per hour. This produces a ceiling effect on both ends of the adrenal spectrum, preventing the catastrophic over-stimulation that kills trauma patients and the crash-to-zero that leaves combatants non-functional after adrenaline depletion.

Street users call it 'The Confessor' because of the uncanny calm it produces — a sense of honest, clear-eyed assessment of whatever situation you're in, stripped of panic and stripped of false courage. Some find this revelatory. Others find it terrifying.

Ringo Corponation Ambient Mesh Leech#

The Ambient Mesh Leech is a passive network parasitism device — a flat, adhesive unit roughly the size of a playing card that attaches to any surface in proximity to active mesh infrastructure and draws communication access from it without registration, authentication, or detectable network presence. It does not connect to the mesh. It infiltrates the connection of something that is already connected, riding the existing authenticated session of a nearby node — a traffic signal, a building management system, a licensed commercial relay — without altering that node's behavior in any measurable way. To the mesh, the Leech does not exist.

Ringo Corponation developed the Leech as an infrastructure audit tool, ostensibly for identifying unauthorized mesh connections by demonstrating how easily they could be established — a rationale that satisfied regulators and provided the legal framework for a product that is, in practice, a highly sophisticated unauthorized access device. The Leech's Phantom Session Architecture generates a synthetic traffic signature that mimics the statistical profile of the host node's normal data throughput, distributing Leech communications invisibly within the host's existing traffic patterns. Extracting the Leech's communications from a captured traffic log requires knowing the Leech's specific session key — without it, the data is indistinguishable from the host node's routine transmissions.

The Leech is a tool of economic necessity as much as operational security. In GLMZ's lower precincts, licensed mesh access is expensive, monitored, and increasingly tiered — the richest users get the cleanest channels, and the poorest make do with degraded public access points that log everything. The Leech provides clean, unmonitored connectivity by stealing it from infrastructure that has already paid for the privilege. This has made it ubiquitous far beyond the criminal and intelligence communities Ringo nominally targets — it is found in community centers, underground clinics, and housing collectives that cannot afford licensed access and will not tolerate surveillance of what little connectivity they have.

Ringo Corponation Composite Surge Frame#

The Composite Surge Frame is Ringo Corponation's entry into the powered exoskeleton market, developed initially for industrial load-bearing applications in Ringo's own logistics and courier infrastructure before being adapted into a protective combat platform. The frame consists of a hardened polymer-composite shell over a motorized titanium alloy skeletal structure, covering the full torso, arms, and legs. Hydraulic micro-actuators augment the wearer's physical strength by a factor of approximately 2.8 and provide load-bearing support that allows the operator to carry armor mass that would be prohibitive without powered assistance. The integrated plating is rated for sustained rifle-caliber fire, making the CSF one of the few commercially available systems offering genuine hard-armor protection to the entire body.

Ringo's engineering philosophy prioritizes durability and repairability over elegance. The CSF uses standardized fastening systems, commercially available hydraulic components, and a modular panel design that allows field replacement of damaged sections using basic tools. This has made the frame remarkably popular in environments far from reliable supply chains — frontier industrial zones, contested territorial borders, and disaster recovery operations where a technician with a socket wrench can keep a frame operational indefinitely. The power system uses a hybrid fuel-cell and capacitor bank that provides 10 hours of standard operation or approximately 4 hours under sustained combat load.

The CSF is bulky, loud in operation, and unmistakably industrial in aesthetic — it does not attempt to conceal itself. Operators in the frame stand roughly 15 centimeters taller than their natural height and move with the deliberate, slightly mechanical gait that hydraulic-assisted movement produces. In GLMZ's street culture, the CSF has become associated with a specific archetype: the heavily built, pragmatic enforcer who values function absolutely over form, and who is prepared to absorb tremendous punishment in exchange for a complete absence of subtlety.

Ringo Corponation Deniable Address Shard#

The Deniable Address Shard is a single-use cryptographic identity chip, roughly the size and shape of a broken fingernail, designed to generate a fully authenticated but entirely fictitious network identity that persists for exactly one communication session before the chip's internal logic physically destroys itself through a controlled electrochemical burn. Each Shard is pre-loaded at manufacture with a unique, non-repeating address seed derived from Ringo Corponation's proprietary entropy architecture, guaranteeing that no two Shards ever produce the same identity. The result is a communication session that, to any network observer, appears to originate from a legitimate registered user — one who simply does not exist.

Ringo Corponation Distributed Mesh Anchor Drone#

The Distributed Mesh Anchor Drone is a compact autonomous aerial platform developed by Ringo Corponation's infrastructure services division for establishing temporary relay and anchor points in environments where fixed infrastructure is absent, compromised, or actively denied. The drone is approximately 28cm in diameter, uses a shrouded quad-rotor configuration for operation in confined spaces, and carries a retractable 40-meter micro-filament tether that can serve as a physical cable guide, a tensioned anchor line, or a hardwire data conduit depending on the filament spool loaded. Once a target anchor point is identified — a structural beam, ventilation housing, or window reveal — the drone fires a spring-loaded micro-grapple and tensions the tether before entering a low-power hover-hold mode that maintains position with minimal noise and battery draw.

Ringo designed the Anchor Drone as a logistics tool for urban infrastructure inspection and repair, where technicians frequently need to route cables or establish working lines across gaps that are impractical to traverse physically. The drone's autonomous anchor-seeking behavior uses a combination of structural density imaging and load-bearing estimation to select anchor points likely to hold working loads, flagging unsuitable targets before committing the grapple. A simple companion app interface allows operators to designate target zones and minimum load ratings without requiring piloting skill, making the device accessible to non-specialist users.

The tether system's versatility has made the Anchor Drone considerably more interesting to operators outside infrastructure services. A hardwire data filament spool transforms the drone into a rapidly deployable physical network bridge across gaps that wireless signals cannot reliably cross — a feature that has not gone unnoticed by individuals for whom wireless transmission is a liability rather than a convenience.

Ringo Corponation Distributed Optic Swarm#

The Distributed Optic Swarm is a reconnaissance drone system consisting of twelve semi-autonomous micro-units, each approximately the size of a large insect, capable of independent navigation and collective mesh-coordinated surveillance. Each unit carries a wide-aperture optical sensor, a short-range acoustic pickup, and a minimal onboard processor running RINGO's SWARM coordination firmware. Individually, each drone is limited — its optics are adequate but not exceptional, its battery life is measured in minutes, and its processing is insufficient for complex autonomous behavior. Collectively, the swarm is a different instrument entirely.

The DOS's engineering distinction is RINGO's COLLECTIVE APERTURE protocol, which treats the twelve optical sensors as a single distributed imaging array. By correlating the slightly different perspectives of drones positioned across a space, the system constructs composite imagery of significantly higher resolution and depth than any single unit could produce. It also enables triangulation of sound sources, detection of active electronic emissions through multi-point signal comparison, and the identification of targets occluded from any individual drone's line of sight. The operator interface is a wrist-mounted display and a neural-adjacent earpiece that translates swarm data into a navigable overview — experienced operators describe controlling the DOS as developing a sense of the space rather than watching a feed.

RINGO CORPONATION markets the DOS primarily to investigative and intelligence clients — journalists, corporate intelligence firms, and private investigation agencies. Its civilian positioning keeps it below the threshold of military equipment regulation in most districts, though security forces have pushed repeatedly to have it reclassified. The swarm's small individual signature makes it exceptionally difficult to detect with standard anti-drone countermeasures, which are calibrated for larger units. The DOS is widely used and widely feared by anyone who needs to maintain operational security in GLMZ's layered interior spaces.

Ringo Corponation Drift Mesh Node#

The Ringo Corponation Drift Mesh Node is a compact, autonomous wireless relay unit designed to be deployed in environments where conventional fixed-infrastructure communication is unavailable, compromised, or under active surveillance. Roughly the size and weight of a large coin, the Drift Node adheres to any surface via micro-suction backing and immediately begins broadcasting a localized mesh relay point that integrates with other Drift Nodes and compatible devices in range, self-organizing into an encrypted peer-to-peer network without any central routing infrastructure. Up to sixty-four nodes can form a single self-healing mesh, automatically rerouting traffic around destroyed or compromised nodes within milliseconds.

Ringo Corponation Fractal Deflection Chassis#

The Fractal Deflection Chassis is a modular hard-plate armor system built on Ringo Corponation's proprietary fractal surface geometry — each plate's exterior is machined into a recursive angular pattern that statistically improves the probability of projectile deflection by altering the angle of incidence across the plate's surface. Unlike conventional flat or curved plates, the fractal geometry means that a round striking anywhere on the plate encounters a micro-angled surface, and a meaningful percentage of rounds that would penetrate a flat plate at a given velocity are instead deflected or tumbled. Ringo's internal testing data, which has been independently contested and partially verified, claims a 22% improvement in deflection rate against standard rifle rounds compared to equivalent-weight flat plate systems.

The modular chassis system uses a standardized attachment rail that allows individual plates to be reconfigured, added, or removed without tools in under two minutes. Ringo markets this as mission-adaptive geometry — operators can prioritize frontal protection, all-around coverage, or a reduced-profile configuration depending on the engagement context. The plates are constructed from a boron carbide and carbon nanotube composite that keeps weight competitive with ceramic alternatives at equivalent protection levels. A color-coding system on each plate's interior face indicates structural integrity, shifting from white to yellow to red as the composite degrades under repeated impacts.

Ringo's background in consumer electronics and communications hardware makes the Chassis an unusual product for a defense market — the company entered personal armor through an acquisition of a small defense materials firm and has approached the category with the modular, user-configurable philosophy that defines its other product lines. The result is a system that experienced operators appreciate for its adaptability and that less experienced users sometimes misconfigure, attaching plates in orientations that create coverage gaps. Ringo's training documentation is thorough but widely ignored.

Ringo Corponation Hollow Channel Communicator#

The Hollow Channel Communicator is a bone-conduction audio device that forgoes all radio transmission in favor of direct physical vibration, transmitting voice communication through contact with any rigid surface — a table, a wall, a vehicle chassis, a railing — that is shared between sender and receiver. Both parties press a small adhesive transducer pad against the same connected physical structure; the sender's voice is converted to vibration, travels through the material, and is reconstructed into audio at the receiver's end. Because the signal never enters the electromagnetic spectrum, it is entirely invisible to radio frequency monitoring, spectrum analysis, and signal intelligence equipment of any kind. There is no transmission to intercept, no frequency to identify, and no encryption to break — because the communication exists only as mechanical vibration within a physical object.

The device's limitations are significant and define its use cases precisely. Both communicating parties must be in contact with the same continuous rigid structure simultaneously, which in practice means the Hollow Channel is used for short-range coordination in confined environments — shared buildings, adjacent rooms, connected vehicles, underground infrastructure. The audio fidelity is acceptable rather than excellent, with some frequency loss through dense or acoustically absorptive materials, and the system cannot carry data, only voice. Ringo Corponation designed the transducer pads to be thin enough to adhere under clothing or inside a jacket lining, making them concealable during covert use.

The Hollow Channel Communicator occupies a niche that other communication tools cannot fill: environments where any electromagnetic emission, however small or encrypted, will trigger automated security responses. High-security corporate vaults, certain government facilities, and the most sensitive private residences in GLMZ are swept continuously for RF activity, making conventional comms suicidal for anyone operating covertly inside them. In these environments, the Hollow Channel is not merely useful — it is the only viable option for maintaining contact between team members.

The device is also used for near-silent communication in surveillance scenarios where even whispered speech carries risk.
cultural context The Hollow Channel Communicator is unrestricted in GLMZ partly because its use cases are narrow enough that it does not register as a threat to the communications monitoring infrastructure that the city's corporate and municipal authorities depend on. It cannot be used to coordinate large groups across distances, it cannot carry data, and it requires physical proximity to a shared structure. What it can do — allow two or three people in the same building to communicate without any detectable signal — is treated as insufficiently dangerous to regulate. This legal status makes it the only professional-grade covert communication tool that can be openly purchased, which in turn has made it a favorite of corporate security consultants who need to demonstrate to clients that their RF-swept facilities can still support internal coordination.

Ringo Corponation Skinline Codec — 'The Thread'#

The Skinline Codec is Ringo Corponation's answer to the problem of communication in fully jammed or surveilled environments: if radio signals can be intercepted and blocked, transmit through something that isn't radio. The Thread uses the body's own bioelectric field as a carrier medium, encoding encrypted data as micro-variations in the skin-surface electrical potential of a user and transmitting it to another Thread user through direct physical contact — a handshake, a touch on the shoulder, a brush of hands. The contact window required is as brief as 0.3 seconds, enough for a full compressed message packet to transfer completely undetected by any external monitoring system.

The hardware consists of two components: a dermal patch worn on the inside of the wrist or palm, and a thumbnail-sized processing unit that clips to the inside of a sleeve or collar. The patch handles signal encoding and skin-coupling; the processing unit handles encryption, message composition, and the haptic feedback pulse that confirms successful transmission. Messages are composed via subvocal input or a paired micro-interface and delivered to the recipient as text or compressed audio on their own interface. Because the transmission medium is the body itself, no signal leaves the participants — it is, in the most literal sense, a communication that exists only between two people touching.

The Thread emerged from Ringo Corponation's courier and logistics division, originally intended for secure package authentication between bonded couriers who needed to confirm handoff without any electronic record. Its adoption by intelligence operatives and underground networks was immediate and predictable. The device has one significant limitation: it only transmits between two users who both carry active units, meaning it requires prior arrangement and cannot be used to reach anyone outside the immediate physical environment. In practice, this limitation has become a feature — a Thread network is inherently small, trust-based, and geographically bounded.

Ringo Corponation Spectral Fold Imager#

The Spectral Fold Imager is a compact multi-band imaging device that captures and computationally 'unfolds' overlapping electromagnetic frequency layers to produce a single composite image containing data from visible light, near-infrared, short-wave infrared, and low-frequency microwave bands simultaneously. The device achieves this through a folded optical path — a series of micro-prism cascades that split incoming light into its constituent frequency ranges and direct each band to a dedicated sensor strip, all within a chassis roughly the size of a hardcover book. The resulting composite image, rendered on the device's high-contrast display, shows a scene with extraordinary informational density: concealed objects, heat sources, electronic emissions, and structural anomalies all visible in a single frame coded by color channel.

Ringo Corponation developed the SFI for their media and surveillance divisions, where the need to capture covert footage in varying light conditions without carrying multiple bulky instruments created a clear market gap. The folded optical path design — Ringo's core innovation — allowed dramatic miniaturization compared to conventional multi-spectral rigs without sacrificing image quality. The device can be operated in 'full composite' mode or narrowed to any single frequency band for targeted analysis. A machine-learning interpretation layer flags anomalies automatically: hidden compartments in walls, warm bodies behind barriers, active electronics in supposedly powered-down equipment.

The SFI has become something of a signature instrument for a specific type of GLMZ operator: the investigative journalist, the corporate intelligence analyst, the high-end infiltrator who needs to see everything a space is hiding before committing to entry. Ringo markets it through their professional imaging division with conspicuous legitimacy, but the device's surveillance capabilities are extensive enough that several districts have moved to restrict its carry without a media or investigative license.

Ringo Corponation Stacked Lens Courier Drone#

The Stacked Lens Courier Drone is a mid-weight autonomous delivery platform built around Ringo Corponation's proprietary multi-aperture optical navigation system — a ring of seven overlapping wide-angle lenses that constructs a continuous 340-degree environmental model updated at 60 frames per second. Unlike conventional drones that rely primarily on LIDAR or GPS, the Stacked Lens uses passive optical triangulation, making it highly resistant to signal jamming and capable of navigating GPS-dark zones such as the Sub-Verge tunnels, shielded corporate campuses, and the electromagnetic noise floors of the Slag Markets. The drone's body is a flattened ovoid roughly the size of a carry case, suspended beneath a contra-rotating six-rotor assembly that minimizes acoustic signature while maintaining lift stability in GLMZ's variable corridor wind conditions.

The drone's most distinctive feature is its adaptive payload cradle — a reconfigurable internal bay that uses the same tensioned band technology found in Ringo Corponation's logistics packaging line. The cradle reads payload weight and geometry on loading and redistributes its internal tension bands to create a custom-fitted, shock-absorbing housing for whatever is placed inside. This makes the Stacked Lens suitable for fragile, irregular, or sensitive cargo that standard drones would damage in transit. A secondary external hardpoint allows attachment of a standardized cargo module for bulk runs, though this significantly increases acoustic signature and reduces maneuverability.

The Stacked Lens occupies a middle ground in GLMZ's drone ecosystem: too large and expensive for casual personal use, too commercially available for exclusive corporate deployment. It is the workhorse of independent courier networks, mid-tier logistics contractors, and — with firmware modifications — a favored platform for runners moving sensitive packages through signal-contested terrain.

Ringo Corponation Tandem Fold Microvan#

The Tandem Fold Microvan is Ringo Corponation's answer to GLMZ's chronic spatial scarcity — a compact urban transport vehicle built around a collapsible chassis system that allows the vehicle to compress its width and length by approximately 40% when parked or navigating narrow corridors. The compression mechanism, called the Tandem Fold System, uses a series of interlocking structural ribs and pneumatic sleeve joints to physically reconfigure the vehicle's profile without compromising the passenger or cargo compartment integrity. In its collapsed state, the Microvan occupies roughly the footprint of a large motorcycle.

tactical use The Microvan's ubiquity is its greatest tactical asset — it blends seamlessly into urban traffic and draws no attention from enforcement or corporate security. Operatives use it as a surveillance vehicle, a mobile staging platform, and a getaway vehicle that can squeeze through alley junctions that would stop a conventional car. The cargo configuration has been used to transport everything from medical supplies to bound prisoners. Its collapsible profile also makes it uniquely suited to rooftop transport, stacked parking facilities, and the compressed transit tunnels that connect certain mid-district blocks.
cultural context The Tandem Fold Microvan is the everyman vehicle of GLMZ — seen everywhere from corporate campus lots to outer-district street markets. It carries no prestige and considerable practicality, which has made it quietly beloved by working residents and quietly contemptuous to the city's upper tiers. Some outer-district communities have developed a culture of extensively modifying Fold Vans into rolling homes, medical clinics, and workshops, given their spatial flexibility. The vehicle appears in dozens of Vantablack Media productions as shorthand for ordinary, struggling urban life.

Sterling-Nakamura Biometric Spoof Kit BSK-2#

A compact kit containing tools for replicating and spoofing biometric authentication systems — fingerprint molds, retinal pattern contact lenses, voice modulation software, and gait adjustment insoles. The BSK-2 starts with a target's biometric data (obtained through surveillance, data breach, or physical collection) and produces physical devices that replicate those biometrics well enough to defeat standard commercial scanners. Sterling-Nakamura Diplomatic Secure Container DSC-5#

A briefcase-sized secure container with integrated biometric lock, tamper detection, and thermite self-destruct system. Sterling-Nakamura issues them to diplomatic staff and high-priority courier services.

Street Custom 'Coffin Nail' Lock Bypass Kit#

A lockpicking and access bypass toolkit assembled from commercially available and custom-fabricated components, contained in a leather roll the size of a pencil case. The kit includes traditional mechanical picks and tension wrenches for pin tumbler locks, an electronic bypass module for keycard systems, a RFID cloner for proximity access, and a compact decoder for electronic combination locks. The electronic components are built on open-source hardware platforms available from any electronics supplier, and the mechanical picks are ground from spring steel by hand. The Coffin Nail is the most common professional lockpicking kit in the lower tiers, and its presence at a scene is considered strong evidence of premeditated unauthorized entry.

The Coyote reads as a purposeful hack—motorcycle DNA evident in the lean chassis, but wildly customized. Handlebars or steering column protrude at odd angles. Battery packs sit exposed or poorly shrouded. No aesthetic unity; function-first design language.
dimensions 2.1–2.8m long, 0.9–1.2m wide, 0.8–1.1m tall depending on configuration (trike vs. quad). Compact enough to thread alleys and service corridors.
weight description 50–150 kg total; light enough for solo transport and evasion, but requires deliberate handling. Handheld carry is impractical; ridden or towed.
primary material Salvaged steel and aluminum motorcycle frames, welded and bolted together. Some plastic fairings (often mismatched or absent). Exposed tubing predominates.
finish Raw welds, patina from multiple lifetimes of use, inconsistent paint jobs or bare metal. Heavy tool marks and modification scars. No factory smoothness.
color scheme Highly variable—primer grey, faded corporate liveries from source machines, flat blacks, rust oranges. Accents of high-visibility tape, electrical harness colors (red/black), and owner customization (graffiti, LED accent strips in cyans and magentas).
interface elements Minimal—basic hand throttle, mechanical brakes (sometimes hydraulic), exposed killswitch. Aftermarket digital dash or jury-rigged phone mount showing charge level. Headlight/taillight often LED salvage. No touchscreen; purely mechanical or basic analog instruments.
distinctive features
  • Visible battery pack modules (cylindrical or rectangular, often duct-taped or clamped to frame)
  • Trailing wiring harnesses—bright colored, poorly sheathed
  • Asymmetrical design—one side pristine salvage, other side modified for fit
  • Custom welded reinforcements and struts at stress points
  • Owner marks: spray-painted callsigns, district gang symbols, or cryptic maintenance notes
  • Mismatched wheels and tires
  • Exposed motor mount with visible cooling fins
manufacturer markings None official. Stamped 'Street Custom' or handwritten builder tag on frame (sometimes hidden). Source components retain faded corp logos (Yamaha, industrial battery house insignia, drone maker marks) beneath modifications.
condition typical Road-worn and actively maintained. Visible dirt from recent rides, fresh welds still dark, tape repairs alongside precision machine work. Smells of ozone, hot metal, and recent electrical work. Evidence of constant tweaking—tools nearby, spare parts strapped to frame.

Street Custom 'Faraday Blanket' EM Shielding Wrap#

A large sheet of conductive fabric that blocks all electromagnetic signals passing through it — wrapping a device, person, or space in the Faraday Blanket creates a complete EM blackout within. The blanket is constructed from copper-nickel mesh woven into a durable fabric backing, flexible enough to wrap around irregular shapes and large enough (2m x 3m) to create a small shielded enclosure. Street operators use it to shield devices from remote tracking, prevent neural interface hacking during sleep, block kill switches in stolen equipment, and create improvised private spaces in surveillance-heavy environments.

Street Custom 'Iron Curtain' Improvised Ballistic Shield#

A ballistic shield fabricated from vehicle door panels, steel plate salvage, or layered industrial materials mounted on improvised handles. The Iron Curtain provides mobile cover against handgun-caliber threats and fragmentary projectiles at a fraction of the cost of commercial ballistic shields. Quality and protection vary enormously, but the cheapest Iron Curtain still beats no cover at all.

Street Custom 'Last Meal' Emergency Ration Fabricator#

A compact device that converts organic waste material — food scraps, plant matter, even paper — into edible nutrient bars through a process of sterilization, chemical breakdown, and reconstitution with added vitamins and binding agents. The Last Meal produces food that is nutritionally complete, bacterially safe, and texturally consistent regardless of input material. It does not taste good — operators describe the output as 'edible cardboard with a chemical aftertaste' — but it sustains life indefinitely from materials that would otherwise be garbage. The device has become essential equipment in Tier 1 where food security is not guaranteed.

Street Custom 'Packrat' Concealed Carry Harness#

A body-worn harness system designed to conceal multiple weapons, tools, and equipment under standard clothing. The Packrat uses a modular design of pouches, holsters, and clips arranged across the torso, inner thighs, and small of back to distribute weight evenly and minimize visible printing through fabric. A well-fitted Packrat can conceal a pistol, three magazines, a knife, a cyberdeck, a medical kit, and assorted tools without creating visible bulges or asymmetric weight distribution. The harness is custom-fitted to the wearer's body and adjustable for different clothing styles. It has become the standard concealment system for anyone who needs to carry lethal capability through areas where weapons are not welcome.

Street Custom 'Trash Armor' Improvised Body Protection#

Body armor improvised from whatever materials are available — layers of duct tape and phone books over vital areas, road sign metal cut into chest plates, layers of ceramic tile taped together, or vehicle floor mats worn as vests. Trash Armor is the protective equipment of people who cannot afford real armor, and its effectiveness varies from surprisingly adequate (layered ceramics can stop handgun rounds) to dangerously inadequate (duct tape and cardboard). The cultural significance of Trash Armor in Tier 1 is that wearing it acknowledges a specific reality: your life is dangerous enough to need armor, and you are poor enough that this is the best you can do.

Tessera Corponation Acoustic Null Field Emitter#

The Acoustic Null Field Emitter is a palm-sized device that projects a directional anti-phase sound field, effectively creating a cone of acoustic cancellation extending up to four meters from the emitter's face. Tessera Corponation's approach differs from conventional white-noise maskers by targeting the precise frequency signatures of the user's movement and speech in real time — an onboard microphone array samples incoming sound at sub-millisecond latency, generates inverted waveforms, and emits them through a phased array of micro-transducers, canceling the user's acoustic output before it propagates beyond the null cone's boundary.

The device's most technically notable characteristic is its adaptive notch filtering, which allows it to suppress the user's sounds while leaving environmental noise largely intact within the cone — meaning the user can still hear their surroundings clearly while remaining acoustically invisible to listeners outside the field. This bidirectional selectivity is computationally intensive and is the primary driver of the unit's relatively short active window on a single charge. At maximum range and fidelity, the emitter sustains approximately ninety minutes of continuous operation before requiring a recharge or cell swap.

Tessera developed the Emitter originally for use by their Lattice network installation crews, who frequently work in acoustically monitored corporate infrastructure. The device moved rapidly into the broader market when early production units were acquired by several high-profile extraction teams and demonstrated in field conditions. Tessera's official position is that the product is sold for 'sensitive facility maintenance applications,' a description that has satisfied regulators in three of GLMZ's six administrative sectors.

Tessera Corponation Ambient Signal Displacement Array#

The Ambient Signal Displacement Array is a palm-sized device worn on the body or placed as a static field emitter that generates a calibrated bubble of electromagnetic interference designed not to block signals — which would itself be detectable — but to displace and scatter them in ways that mimic natural environmental noise. Where crude jammers create a dead zone that passive monitoring systems immediately flag as an anomaly, the Array samples the ambient signal environment within its operational radius and synthesizes a layered output of false signals, reflections, and interference patterns that make the area appear, to any external monitoring system, as a region of ordinary urban electromagnetic clutter.

Tessera developed the Array's core displacement architecture from research into urban signal mapping — specifically, the problem of predicting how dense city infrastructure affects wireless propagation. The same models that predict signal behavior can be run in reverse to generate convincing synthetic scatter. The Array updates its output profile every 200 milliseconds, adapting to changes in the ambient signal environment to maintain the illusion of naturalness. This makes it effective not only against real-time monitoring but against retrospective signal forensics, since the Array's emissions blend into baseline environmental noise in recorded data.

The device has a secondary function that its documentation quietly omits: at close range, it disrupts the short-range biometric handshake protocols that many corporate access and identification systems use to passively scan nearby individuals. This means that personnel within the Array's radius may fail to register on proximity-based attendance or identity logging systems — a function that makes the Array quietly indispensable for anyone who needs to be somewhere without their presence being logged, without the overt aggression of a full signal jam.

Tessera Corponation Cenotaph Burst Transmitter — 'The Epitaph'#

The Cenotaph Burst Transmitter is a single-use emergency communications device — a hardened cylinder approximately the size of a flare, designed to transmit one compressed message packet across a maximum possible range before destroying itself. Tessera Corponation developed it for deep-cover operatives and isolated field agents who needed a last-resort option when all other communication had failed. The device charges over a period of 60–90 seconds from activation, during which it compresses, encrypts, and fractures the stored message into a multi-frequency burst transmission that fires simultaneously across forty-three frequency bands in a single 0.008-second pulse.

The burst is, by design, impossible to miss and impossible to trace. The transmission is so brief that direction-finding equipment cannot lock a bearing before it ends; the multi-frequency fracturing means no single monitoring system captures the complete message; and the device physically incinerates its own internals after firing, leaving a slag of ceramic and fused circuitry that yields nothing recoverable. Recipients must have a Tessera Cenotaph receiver unit — a small passive module that captures and reconstructs burst fragments across all forty-three bands simultaneously — to decode the message. Without a paired receiver, the burst is unintelligible noise across dozens of bands.

The Epitaph's cultural weight comes from its irreversibility. A device that destroys itself after a single transmission, designed for use when everything else has failed, carries an unmistakable implication. Tessera markets it to corporations for deniable deep-cover operations; the black market sells it to anyone who thinks they might someday need to scream once, very loudly, and then disappear. In GLMZ intelligence circles, receiving an Epitaph burst from a contact is understood to mean one of two things: either they've gone dark permanently, or whatever they've just told you is the most important thing they'll ever say.

Tessera Corponation Gradient Veil Transceiver#

The Gradient Veil Transceiver is a palm-sized communications device built around Tessera's Spectral Smear Engine — a hardware-level signal processor that distributes a single transmission across dozens of simultaneous frequency bands at varying power levels, creating what appears on any monitoring sweep as uniform low-level atmospheric noise rather than a coherent broadcast. The receiving unit uses the same Spectral Smear key to reassemble the dispersed signal in real time, producing clean audio output. Without the matching key, the transmission is acoustically and mathematically indistinguishable from interference.

The device is built into a matte-black chassis roughly the size of a cigarette case, with a recessed dial for manual key cycling and a single flush-mounted speaker grille. It pairs with a standard throat mic or a dedicated lapel pickup. The Gradient Veil operates entirely in hardware — there is no software stack to exploit, no firmware to patch, and no network handshake to intercept. Tessera designed it specifically for environments where digital encryption is considered a liability because it can be cracked, spoofed, or exploited through software vulnerabilities.

Tessera Corponation Laminar Ghost Chassis#

The Laminar Ghost Chassis is Tessera Corponation's flagship stealth suit — a full-body garment system that combines passive thermal baffling, acoustic dampening laminate, and a dynamic optical surface layer into a unified platform. The outer surface is composed of Tessera's proprietary Fold-Reactive polymer, which samples ambient light from micro-aperture sensors distributed across the suit and re-emits it through a micro-LED matrix on the opposing surface, creating a near-real-time visual camouflage effect that is effective against human observers and most standard optical surveillance systems at ranges beyond four meters. The effect degrades noticeably at close range and breaks down entirely under ultraviolet or multispectral scanning.

Beneath the optical layer, the Ghost Chassis incorporates a passive thermal baffling membrane that suppresses the wearer's infrared signature to approximately ambient temperature within 90 seconds of activation, and an acoustic dampening laminate that reduces movement noise to below 15 decibels at normal walking pace. The suit is powered by a distributed micro-cell array woven through the lining, providing up to six hours of full active operation before requiring recharge. Tessera has positioned the Ghost Chassis as an intelligence-gathering and infiltration tool rather than a combat platform — the underlying armor protection is modest, rated for light fragmentation and minimal ballistic resistance.

The Ghost Chassis is tightly controlled by Tessera, sold exclusively through authorized intelligence-sector procurement channels and issued under strict end-user licensing agreements. Despite this, several units have surfaced in the hands of corporate espionage teams, high-end criminal organizations, and at least one documented case involving a GLMZ investigative journalist who used one to document a restricted Tessera research facility — an incident that resulted in significant legal action and the journalist's disappearance.

tactical use The Ghost Chassis is optimized for reconnaissance, infiltration, and exfiltration in controlled environments. Operators are trained to move slowly and deliberately — rapid movement creates artifacts in the optical layer that are detectable even at range. The suit is most effective in low-light conditions where the optical camouflage is supplemented by natural shadow. Standard counter-tactics include UV flood lighting, multispectral scanning sweeps, and acoustic sensors below the suit's dampening threshold.
cultural context The Ghost Chassis exists in a space of near-mythological status in GLMZ's intelligence and criminal communities. Its rarity and the legal risk of possessing one make it a symbol of extreme capability and resource. Tessera's aggressive enforcement of end-user agreements — including rumored remote-deactivation and self-destruct capabilities built into the power array — means that owning one outside of sanctioned channels is understood to be a direct confrontation with the corporation. Some operators refer to unsanctioned Ghost Chassis units as 'orphans,' acknowledging their precarious status.
